<a id="s0-p1"></a>[0¶1] This document defines the regular-expression language `pcrec` compiles: every construct it accepts, what each one matches, which captures it sets and in what preference order, which module gates it, how it is refused when it is not available, and how the encoding and the compile options change any of that. It is pcrec's own contract. `docs/pcre2_compliance.md` is the delta from PCRE2, construct by construct; `pcrec --list-syntax` is the generated construct index (`registry.md` §2) and §10 below is checked against it row for row. The match API that runs a compiled pattern is `match_api.md`; the command line is `cli.md`; the numeric limits are `limits.md`; the `.rxt` source format is `rxt_format.md`; module `vars` has its own document, `vars.md`. The history of this document is `docs/dev/history/pattern_language_record.md`, which is not normative.

<a id="s0-p2"></a>[0¶2] Every sentence below that says what a pattern matches can be checked by compiling the pattern and running it. Examples are written `PATTERN` on `SUBJECT` → `[start, end)` for the whole-match span, followed by group spans where they matter; `-1` is an unset group (`match_api.md` §5). Subjects are written with the escapes of `rxt_format.md` (`\n`, `\xHH`). Unless an example names an option, it is compiled with the bare defaults: `-e byte`, no `-i`, `--features` absent (so `std1`, §2.3), `--engine=auto`, captures on.

<a id="s1"></a>
## 1. Scope, reference and tiers

<a id="s1-1"></a>
### 1.1 What this document defines

<a id="s1-1-p1"></a>[1.1¶1] A pattern is a sequence of bytes given to one compile (`cli.md` §1.3, `match_api.md` §7) together with that compile's options. This document defines, for every pattern and option set, whether the compile is accepted, and for an accepted one, which spans and captures a search reports on every subject. It does not define the emitted C, the entry points, the give-up codes or the budgets; those are `match_api.md` and `limits.md`, and this document names them only where a construct's behaviour depends on them.

<a id="s1-2"></a>
### 1.2 The reference semantics

<a id="s1-2-p1"></a>[1.2¶1] For every construct this document describes as matching "as PCRE2", the answer is libpcre2's answer at the corresponding PCRE2 options, and the reference build is libpcre2 10.46 with its default compile-time configuration (newline LF, `\R` any Unicode newline, Unicode 16.0.0 tables in pcrec):

| pcrec compile | PCRE2 compile options | PCRE2 match options |
|---|---|---|
| `-e byte` (default) | `0` (8-bit, non-UTF) | `0` |
| `-e utf8` | `PCRE2_UTF` | `0`, with `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` semantics for an ill-formed subject (`match_api.md` §9.3) |
| `-i` | adds `PCRE2_CASELESS` | |
| `--ucp`, or `(*UCP)` | adds `PCRE2_UCP` | |

<a id="s1-2-p2"></a>[1.2¶2] A search from `startpos` corresponds to `pcre2_match` at start offset `startpos`. Where pcrec's answer differs from libpcre2's at that mapping, the difference is stated where the construct is defined and collected in §9. A difference that is not stated is a defect.

<a id="s1-3"></a>
### 1.3 The contract tiers

1. <a id="s1-3-p1"></a>[1.3¶1] What an accepted pattern matches — the span, every group's span, and whether a search finds a match at all — is exact. A wrong answer is always a defect.
2. <a id="s1-3-p2"></a>[1.3¶2] Whether a construct is accepted, and which module owns it, is exact: the module named in a refusal is the module that owns the construct, and a construct PCRE2 accepts is either accepted, or refused by one of the refusal shapes of §2.4, never accepted with a different meaning; the one pcrec extension, module `vars`' `${`, is §7.10.
3. <a id="s1-3-p3"></a>[1.3¶3] pcrec's own pattern offset in a diagnostic is exact under pcrec's own convention (`cli.md` §3.3¶4).
4. <a id="s1-3-p4"></a>[1.3¶4] The wording of a diagnostic is not part of this contract, except the substring `requires module 'X'` and the other shape markers of §2.4. PCRE2's error numbers and offsets are never promised.

<a id="s1-4"></a>
### 1.4 Reading a construct table

<a id="s1-4-p1"></a>[1.4¶1] Each construct section has a table with these columns. `spelling` is the construct as written; where it is also a `--list-syntax` row's `syntax`, §10 names the section. `matches` is the meaning. `module` is the gate (§2.3): `base` means no module. `engines` is which engine can run the construct in general: `any` for either, `vm` for the backtracking VM only; a `vm` construct may still compile under `--engine=dfa` when the pattern is rewritten into an equivalent the DFA can run (§4.5). `quantifiable` says whether a quantifier may follow the construct (§5.6); a construct that cannot be quantified refuses `X*` with "quantifier does not follow a repeatable item".

<a id="s2"></a>
## 2. What selects the language

<a id="s2-1"></a>
### 2.1 The pattern text

<a id="s2-1-p1"></a>[2.1¶1] The pattern is a byte string. It cannot contain a NUL byte, because the compile entry takes no pattern length (`cli.md` §1.4¶3); `\x00` is the spelling of a NUL character (§5.2).

<a id="s2-1-p2"></a>[2.1¶2] Under `-e byte` every byte is one pattern character, and a byte `0x80`-`0xFF` is a literal character with that code point. Under `-e utf8` the pattern must be well-formed UTF-8: an ill-formed sequence is refused with "ill-formed UTF-8 in pattern" at the offset of the sequence (`\xff` refuses at offset 0; `a\xc3` refuses at offset 1), and a well-formed multi-byte sequence is one character.

<a id="s2-2"></a>
### 2.2 The encoding

<a id="s2-2-p1"></a>[2.2¶1] `-e byte` and `-e utf8` select what a CHARACTER of the subject is (`match_api.md` §9.1, `cli.md` §1.7):

| | `byte` | `utf8` |
|---|---|---|
| a character is | one byte, code point `0x00`-`0xFF` | one well-formed UTF-8 sequence, code point `U+0000`-`U+10FFFF` except surrogates |
| `.`, a class, `\N`, a negated escape match | one byte | one whole character, 1 to 4 bytes |
| `\x{h...}` above `0xFF` | refused, naming the encoding | accepted up to `10FFFF`; `D800`-`DFFF` refused |
| an ill-formed subject sequence | cannot occur | matched by nothing (`match_api.md` §9.3), or refused under `-futf-check` (`match_api.md` §9.4) |
| default meaning of `\d \s \w`, POSIX classes, `\b` | ASCII sets | ASCII sets |
| `\h \H \v \V` | `[\t \xa0]`, `[\n\x0b\f\r\x85]` and their complements | PCRE2_UTF's Unicode lists (`cli.md` §1.9¶3) |
| `-i` fold | the 52 ASCII letters | Unicode simple case folding (`cli.md` §1.8) |
| modules implied on | none | `unicode-props` and `ucp` (§2.3) |

<a id="s2-2-p2"></a>[2.2¶2] So `.` on `é` (the bytes `\xc3\xa9`) is `[0, 1)` under `byte` and `[0, 2)` under `utf8`; `é+` under `byte` is `\xc3` followed by one or more `\xa9`, and under `utf8` one or more `é`.

<a id="s2-3"></a>
### 2.3 The module gate

<a id="s2-3-p1"></a>[2.3¶1] Every construct outside the base tier (§5) belongs to exactly one module, named in `--list-syntax`'s `module` column. A compile enables a set of modules; a construct whose module is not enabled is refused with `requires module 'X'`.

- <a id="s2-3-p2"></a>[2.3¶2] The set is chosen by `--features LIST` (`cli.md` §1.17) or `pcrec_options.features` (`match_api.md` §8.2). `LIST` is either a comma-separated list of module names, or exactly one of `std1`, `all` or `none`; a named set does not combine with module names (`--features std1,quoting` is refused as an unknown module `std1`).
- <a id="s2-3-p3"></a>[2.3¶3] With no `--features`, the set is `std1` = {`classes`, `modifiers`}. An explicit list REPLACES `std1`; it does not add to it: `--features named-groups` compiles `(?<n>a)` and refuses `\d` and `(?i)`.
- <a id="s2-3-p4"></a>[2.3¶4] `-e utf8` enables `unicode-props` and `ucp` in addition to whatever the list names.
- <a id="s2-3-p5"></a>[2.3¶5] `--features none` enables nothing: `\d`, `[[:digit:]]`, `[\d]` and `(?i)` are refused, naming `classes` and `modifiers`.
- <a id="s2-3-p5a"></a>[2.3¶5a] The gate governs pattern SYNTAX, not compile options: `-i` (`PCREC_CASELESS`) works under every feature set, `--features none` included, because case folding is base machinery and `(?i)` is only the modifiers module's spelling of it (§6.2¶4). `--ucp` is the exception, refused without module `ucp`, because it changes what `\d \s \w \b` mean and only that module implements the change (§7.8).

<a id="s2-3-p6"></a>[2.3¶6] A module whose construct has no producer in this build refuses the construct even when enabled (§2.4, shape 2). §6 and §7 are the modules with producers; §8 lists the rest.

<a id="s2-4"></a>
### 2.4 Refusals

<a id="s2-4-p1"></a>[2.4¶1] A refused compile writes nothing and exits 1 (`cli.md` §3.1); the library entry returns its error (`match_api.md` §7). Every refusal names an offset into the pattern. The shapes, by the marker the diagnostic carries:

| shape | marker in the diagnostic | means |
|---|---|---|
| 1 gated | `requires module 'X'` | the construct is real and owned by module `X`, which this compile did not enable (module `verbs` uses this shape at every gate state, §8.1) |
| 2 unbuilt | `module 'X' is enabled but ... is not implemented yet` | `X` is enabled and has no producer for this construct |
| 3 out of scope | `is outside pcrec's scope and no module will implement it` | real PCRE2 syntax pcrec excludes permanently (§8.2) |
| 4 engine | `requires the VM engine, which --engine=dfa excludes` | the construct (as rewritten, §4.5) needs the VM and `--engine=dfa` was requested |
| 5 capability | a sentence naming what is not implemented | the construct is accepted by PCRE2, pcrec owns it, and this instance is beyond what pcrec builds (variable-length lookbehind, §7.4; wide UCP sets, §7.8) |
| 6 resource | a sentence naming the budget and its raise flag | a compile-time budget was exceeded (`limits.md` §3.3) |
| 7 grammar | a PCRE2-like sentence | the pattern is not well-formed; PCRE2 refuses it too |

<a id="s2-4-p2"></a>[2.4¶2] Shape 7's wording follows PCRE2's where pcrec has one to follow, and that is a courtesy, not a contract (§1.3).

<a id="s2-5"></a>
### 2.5 Options that change meaning

<a id="s2-5-p1"></a>[2.5¶1] These compile options change what a pattern means. Every other option (the `-f` family, `--tune`, `--part-*`, `--memfn`, the budgets) changes how the artifact is built and never an answer, except by moving where a give-up or a resource refusal happens.

| option | inline spelling | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `-i` | `(?i)` at pattern start | caseless matching, §6.2 and `cli.md` §1.8 |
| `--ucp` | `(*UCP)` at pattern start | Unicode semantics for `\d \s \w \b`, POSIX classes, §7.8 |
| `-e utf8` | `(*UTF)` / `(*UTF8)` confirm it; they cannot select it | §2.2 |
| `--features` | none | §2.3 |
| `--no-captures` | none | every group is reported as if non-capturing; only `[start, end)` is written (`cli.md` §1.11) |
| `--engine=dfa\|vm\|auto` | none | never an answer; a request the pattern cannot honour is refused (§4.5) |

<a id="s2-5-p2"></a>[2.5¶2] `(?m)`, `(?s)`, `(?x)`, `(?xx)`, `(?n)`, `(?U)`, `(?J)`, `(?a…)` and `(?r)` have no command-line flag; a `.rxt` block's `flags` line (`rxt_format.md` §1.5¶4) carries the letters.

<a id="s3"></a>
## 3. Grammar

<a id="s3-1"></a>
### 3.1 Structure

<a id="s3-1-p1"></a>[3.1¶1] The grammar below fixes structure and precedence; each terminal is defined by the section named beside it. Quantifiers bind tighter than concatenation, which binds tighter than `|`.

```
pattern      = { start-option } alternation ;                (* §7.8, §8.1 *)
alternation  = branch { "|" branch } ;                        (* §5.7 *)
branch       = { item } ;                                     (* may be empty *)
item         = atom [ quantifier ]                            (* §5.6 *)
             | option-setting ;                               (* (?i) and friends, §6.2 *)
quantifier   = ( "*" | "+" | "?" | braces ) [ "?" | "+" ] ;  (* "+" suffix: §7.2 *)
braces       = "{" sp digits sp "}"
             | "{" sp digits sp "," sp [ digits ] sp "}"
             | "{" sp "," sp digits sp "}" ;                  (* sp = zero or more space/tab *)
atom         = literal | escape | "." | class | group
             | "^" | "$" | ...                                (* every construct of §5-§8 *)
group        = "(" alternation ")"                            (* capturing, §5.7 *)
             | "(?:" alternation ")"                          (* non-capturing, §5.7 *)
             | "(?" option-letters ":" alternation ")"        (* scoped options, §6.2 *)
             | "(?" ... ")"                                   (* every other (? group, §7-§8 *)
```

<a id="s3-1-p2"></a>[3.1¶2] A `{` that does not begin one of the three `braces` forms is a literal `{` (`a{`, `a{x}`, `a{,}` and `a{1 2}` match themselves), and `}` and `]` outside a class are literals. Some atoms are not quantifiable (§1.4), and a `quantifier` directly after another `quantifier` is refused ("multiple quantifiers on the same item": `a**`, `a{2}{3}`), except that the single `?` or `+` suffix is part of the first quantifier.

<a id="s3-2"></a>
### 3.2 Extended mode

<a id="s3-2-p1"></a>[3.2¶1] Under `(?x)` (§6.2), outside a class and outside `\Q…\E`, the whitespace characters `\t \n \x0b \f \r`, space and U+0085 (under `-e byte` the byte `\x85`) are ignored, and under `-e utf8` also U+200E, U+200F, U+2028 and U+2029 (§3.2¶2), and `#` begins a comment that ends at the next `\n` (or the end of the pattern). Whitespace is ignored between items and between a quantifier and its `?`/`+` suffix (`(?x)a+ ?` is `a+?`), but not inside a token: `(?x)( ?:a)` is a group starting with a quantifier, refused, and `(?x)(? i)` is refused. Inside braces only space and tab are allowed in any mode (§3.1). An escaped space, `\ `, is a literal space. `(?xx)` additionally ignores space and tab inside a class (`(?xx)[ a]` matches `a` and not a space).

<a id="s3-2-p2"></a>[3.2¶2] Under `-e utf8` the ignored set is Unicode's Pattern_White_Space, read as characters: `(?x)a`, U+2028, `b` (the pattern bytes `(?x)a\xe2\x80\xa8b`) on `ab` → `[0, 2)`. Under `-e byte` no character exceeds `\xff`, so the same bytes are three literals there. A comment still ends only at `\n`, and `(?xx)` still ignores only space and tab inside a class.

<a id="s4"></a>
## 4. Matching

<a id="s4-1"></a>
### 4.1 Which match a search reports

<a id="s4-1-p1"></a>[4.1¶1] A search from `startpos` (`match_api.md` §3.1) reports the match at the smallest position `p >= startpos` at which the pattern matches, and at `p`, the first successful way of matching in the preference order of §4.2. That is the match PCRE2's backtracking matcher reports. It is not the longest match: `a|ab` on `ab` is `[0, 1)`, and `ab|a` is `[0, 2)`.

<a id="s4-2"></a>
### 4.2 Preference order

<a id="s4-2-p1"></a>[4.2¶1] The ways a pattern can match at one position are ordered, and the first that succeeds is the match:

1. <a id="s4-2-p2"></a>[4.2¶2] Alternatives are tried left to right.
2. <a id="s4-2-p3"></a>[4.2¶3] A greedy quantifier tries more iterations before fewer; a lazy one (`*?`, `+?`, `??`, `{n,m}?`) fewer before more. `(?U)` swaps the two spellings (§6.2).
3. <a id="s4-2-p4"></a>[4.2¶4] A possessive quantifier and an atomic group (§7.2) keep the first way their body matched and never try another.
4. <a id="s4-2-p5"></a>[4.2¶5] Concatenation orders lexicographically: an earlier item's choice is changed only after every choice of the later items has failed.

<a id="s4-2-p6"></a>[4.2¶6] `(a|ab)(c|bcd)(d*)` on `abcd` → `[0, 4)`, group 1 `[0, 1)`, group 2 `[1, 4)`, group 3 `[4, 4)`. `a*?b` on `aaab` → `[0, 4)`. `a{2,3}?` on `aaaa` → `[0, 2)`.

<a id="s4-3"></a>
### 4.3 Empty iterations

<a id="s4-3-p1"></a>[4.3¶1] An iteration of a quantified item that matches the empty string ends the repetition: no further iteration is tried after it. `(a*)*b` on `b` → `[0, 1)`, group 1 `[0, 0)`; `(|a)+` on `aa` → `[0, 0)`, group 1 `[0, 0)`; `(|a)+$` on `aa` → `[0, 2)`, group 1 `[2, 2)`.

<a id="s4-4"></a>
### 4.4 Captures

<a id="s4-4-p1"></a>[4.4¶1] A capturing group is numbered by the position of its opening parenthesis, counting from 1, left to right through the whole pattern, including groups inside lookarounds and inside groups that never run. A group holds the span of its last execution on the reported path, and keeps a value from an earlier iteration of an enclosing quantifier when its own iteration did not run it (`match_api.md` §5.1): `((a)|(b))*` on `ab` → group 1 `[1, 2)`, group 2 `[0, 1)`, group 3 `[1, 2)`. A group that never ran on the reported path is unset. `(a)|b` on `b` → group 1 unset. `(a{0})b` on `b` → group 1 `[0, 0)`: a zero-count repeat inside the group still runs the group. How spans are delivered, and what `--no-captures` changes, is `match_api.md` §5 and `cli.md` §1.11; how named groups and library groups are numbered is §7.5 and `match_api.md` §5.4-§5.5.

<a id="s4-5"></a>
### 4.5 Engines never change an answer

<a id="s4-5-p1"></a>[4.5¶1] pcrec has two engines: a DFA, which cannot run captures or any `vm` construct, and a backtracking VM, which can run everything this document accepts (`cli.md` §1.13). `--engine=auto` (the default) chooses; the choice never changes an answer. Some `vm` constructs are rewritten when the pattern allows an exact equivalent the DFA can run, so whether a given pattern compiles under `--engine=dfa --no-captures` depends on the whole pattern, not only on its constructs: `(?=a)a` and `\w+(?=\d)` compile under `--engine=dfa --no-captures`, `(?=.*b)a` is refused with shape 4. The rewrites and their deny flags are `tuning.md` §2.8 and §2.9. A capture-bearing pattern under `--engine=dfa` without `--no-captures` is refused.

<a id="s4-6"></a>
### 4.6 Give-ups

<a id="s4-6-p1"></a>[4.6¶1] A VM artifact may return a give-up code instead of an answer when it exhausts a budget or a capacity (`limits.md` §2): `PCREC_ERR_STEPS`, `PCREC_ERR_FRAMES`, `PCREC_ERR_WORK`. A give-up is never a wrong answer and is not a difference from PCRE2 under this document's tiers; it says nothing about whether the subject matches. A DFA artifact never gives up.

<a id="s5"></a>
## 5. The base tier

<a id="s5-p1"></a>[5¶1] The base tier is the grammar every compile accepts, whatever `--features` says, including `--features none`. Its constructs have no `--list-syntax` row, except `^`, `$`, `(...)`, `(?:...)` and the character escapes, which have rows with `status` `base` (§10).

<a id="s5-1"></a>
### 5.1 Literal characters

<a id="s5-1-p1"></a>[5.1¶1] Outside a class, every character except the metacharacters `\ ^ $ . [ | ( ) * + ?` and a `{` that begins a quantifier (§3.1) is a literal that matches itself; under `(?x)`, whitespace and `#` are not literals either (§3.2). `]`, `}` and a `{` that begins no quantifier are literals. A `)` with no open group is refused ("unmatched closing parenthesis"), and an unclosed `(` is refused ("missing closing )").

<a id="s5-1-p2"></a>[5.1¶2] A literal matches exactly the character it is, compared by code point; under `-i` it also matches its case partners (§6.2). Under `-e byte` a non-ASCII byte in the pattern is one literal byte; under `-e utf8` a non-ASCII character is one literal character (`é+` on `éé` → `[0, 4)`).

<a id="s5-2"></a>
### 5.2 Character escapes

| spelling | matches | module |
|---|---|---|
| `\a` | U+0007 | base |
| `\e` | U+001B | base |
| `\f` | U+000C | base |
| `\n` | U+000A | base |
| `\r` | U+000D | base |
| `\t` | U+0009 | base |
| `\xh`, `\xhh` | the code point given by one or two hex digits; a third hex digit is a literal (`\x412` is `A` then `2`) | base |
| `\x{h...}` | the code point given by one or more hex digits, leading zeros allowed; at most `FF` under `byte`, `10FFFF` and not `D800`-`DFFF` under `utf8` | base |
| `\` + a character that is not an ASCII letter or digit | that character (`\.`, `\\`, `\{`, `\_`, `\ `, and under `utf8` `\é`) | base |
| `\0`, `\0o`, `\0oo` | octal: the code point of the octal digits, at most three digits counting the `0` (`\0377` is U+001F then `7`) | `backrefs` (§7.3) |
| `\ddd` | a backreference or an octal escape, by the rule of §7.3 | `backrefs` |
| `\cX`, `\o{...}` | a control character, an octal code point | `misc`, not built (§8.1) |
| `\N{U+h...}` | a code point by number | `unicode-props`, not built (§8.1) |

<a id="s5-2-p1"></a>[5.2¶1] `\x` with no hex digit after it, and `\x{` with no hex digit or a non-hex character before `}`, are refused. Spaces and tabs may stand between `{` and the digits and between the digits and `}`, never among the digits: `\x{ 41 }` is `A`, `\x{4 1}` is refused. Inside a class the same escapes have the same meanings, and the octal and digit escapes are base-tier there (§5.5).

<a id="s5-2-p2"></a>[5.2¶2] An octal escape's value is range-checked like `\x{...}`'s, against the encoding: above `\377` (`\400`-`\777`, U+0100-U+01FF) it is refused under `byte` ("octal value is greater than \377") and accepted under `utf8`, in a class, outside one, and as the octal reading of the digit rule (§7.3¶2): `(a)\400` under `utf8` is `a` then U+0100.

<a id="s5-3"></a>
### 5.3 Refused escapes

<a id="s5-3-p1"></a>[5.3¶1] A backslash followed by an ASCII letter that names no construct is refused ("unknown escape"): `\i \j \l \m \q \u \y \F \I \J \L \M \O \T \U \Y`. A backslash at the end of the pattern is refused. The letters that do name constructs are defined in this document: `\a \e \f \n \r \t \x` (§5.2), `\d \D \h \H \s \S \v \V \w \W \N` (§6.1), `\b \B \A \Z \z \G \K` (§7.1), `\g \k` and the digits (§7.3, §7.7), `\Q \E` (§7.6), `\p \P` (§7.9), `\c \o \C \R \X` (§8.1).

<a id="s5-4"></a>
### 5.4 Dot

<a id="s5-4-p1"></a>[5.4¶1] `.` matches any one character except U+000A (`\n`); under `(?s)` (§6.2) it matches any character. Under `byte` that is any byte but `\n`, `\x85` and `\r` included; under `utf8` any well-formed character but `\n`, U+0085 and U+2028 included. `.` never matches an ill-formed byte.

<a id="s5-5"></a>
### 5.5 Character classes

<a id="s5-5-p1"></a>[5.5¶1] `[...]` matches one character in the set its body describes; `[^...]` matches one character not in it. A negated class matches `\n` (`[^a]` on `\n` → `[0, 1)`), and under `utf8` it matches only well-formed characters.

1. <a id="s5-5-p2"></a>[5.5¶2] A `]` immediately after `[` or `[^` is a member, not the terminator: `[]a]` matches `]` and `a`; `[^]a]` matches neither. `[]` with no later `]` is refused ("missing terminating ]"), as is any class with no terminator.
2. <a id="s5-5-p3"></a>[5.5¶3] `x-y` is a range of code points from `x` to `y` inclusive; `x` and `y` may be literals or single-character escapes (`[\x{41}-\x{43}]`, `[\t-\r]`, `[a-\x{7a}]`). A range with `y < x` is refused ("range out of order"). A range whose endpoint is a set (`[\d-z]`, `[a-\d]`, `[\w-.]`, `[[:alpha:]-z]`) is refused ("invalid range").
3. <a id="s5-5-p4"></a>[5.5¶4] A `-` that cannot start or end a range is a literal: first (`[-a]`), last (`[a-]`), or right after a range (`[a-c-e]` matches `a`-`c` and `-`, not `d`).
4. <a id="s5-5-p5"></a>[5.5¶5] The character escapes of §5.2 mean the same inside a class. Escapes that are different inside a class: `\b` is U+0008; `\0`-`\7` begin an octal escape of up to three octal digits (a value above `\377` is a code point up to U+01FF under `utf8` and is refused under `byte`, §5.2¶2); `\8`, `\9`, `\g` and `\k` are the literal letters (`[\k<n>]` matches `k`, `<`, `n` and `>`); `\` + a non-alphanumeric character is that character. These are base-tier inside a class even though the same spellings outside a class belong to `backrefs`.
5. <a id="s5-5-p6"></a>[5.5¶6] Refused inside a class: `\B \A \Z \z \G \K \R \X` ("not valid inside a character class"), `\N`, and an unknown escape (`[\y]`).
6. <a id="s5-5-p7"></a>[5.5¶7] `[:name:]` inside a class is a POSIX class (§6.1, module `classes`); `[:name:]` outside a class is refused ("only valid inside a character class"). `[.x.]` and `[=x=]` inside a class are refused ("POSIX collating elements are not supported"), as PCRE2 refuses them.
7. <a id="s5-5-p8"></a>[5.5¶8] The class escapes `\d \D \s \S \w \W \h \H \v \V` inside a class add their sets (§6.1, module `classes`). `\p{...}` and `\P{...}` add a property set (§7.9). `\Q...\E` inside a class quotes its contents as members (§7.6, module `quoting`); a lone `\E` in a class needs `quoting` too.
8. <a id="s5-5-p9"></a>[5.5¶9] `&&`, `--` and `~~` have no set-operation meaning: `[a&&b]` matches `a`, `&` and `b`. The set-operation class syntax is `(?[...])` (§8.1).
9. <a id="s5-5-p10"></a>[5.5¶10] Under `-i` the set is closed under the encoding's case fold (`cli.md` §1.8); a negated class negates the folded set (`(?i)[^a]` does not match `A`).

<a id="s5-6"></a>
### 5.6 Quantifiers

| spelling | iterations | preference |
|---|---|---|
| `X*` | 0 or more | greedy |
| `X+` | 1 or more | greedy |
| `X?` | 0 or 1 | greedy |
| `X{n}` | exactly n | — |
| `X{n,}`, `X{n, }` | n or more | greedy |
| `X{n,m}` | n to m | greedy |
| `X{,m}` | 0 to m | greedy |
| any of the above + `?` | the same | lazy |
| any of the above + `+` | the same | possessive (greedy, whatever `(?U)` says), module `atomic-groups` (§7.2) |

1. <a id="s5-6-p1"></a>[5.6¶1] `n` and `m` are decimal, at most 65535 (`PCREC_MAX_REPEAT`); a larger number is refused ("number too big"), and `m < n` is refused ("numbers out of order"). Leading zeros are allowed. Space and tab may surround the numbers and the comma (`a{ 1 , 2 }`); any other character inside makes the `{` a literal (§3.1).
2. <a id="s5-6-p2"></a>[5.6¶2] A quantifier with nothing before it in its branch (`*a`, `a|*b`, `(*a`, `{1}`) is refused ("quantifier does not follow a repeatable item"), as is one after a construct whose `quantifiable` is `no` (§1.4): `^*`, `a$?`, `\b*`, `\K+`. `(^)*` and `(?:$)?` are groups and are quantifiable, and so is a group whose whole body is an option setting: `(?:(?i))*a`, `((?s))?a` and `(?=(?m))+a` compile, the group matching the empty string and its option change ending at its `)`, so `(?:(?i))*a` matches `a` and not `A`. The option setting itself is not quantifiable (`a(?i)*` is refused).
3. <a id="s5-6-p3"></a>[5.6¶3] A large bounded count can exceed a compile budget and be refused with a resource shape (§2.4): `a{0,65535}` exceeds `PCREC_MAX_NFA_STATES` at the default (`limits.md` §3.3).
4. <a id="s5-6-p4"></a>[5.6¶4] `X{0}` matches the empty string, and a group inside it is reported as `[p, p)` where `p` is the position (§4.4). `(?:){3}` matches the empty string.

<a id="s5-7"></a>
### 5.7 Alternation and groups

<a id="s5-7-p1"></a>[5.7¶1] `A|B` matches what `A` matches or what `B` matches, `A` preferred (§4.2). Either side may be empty: `a||b` on `xb` → `[0, 0)`, the empty middle alternative winning at position 0.

| spelling | matches | captures |
|---|---|---|
| `(X)` | `X` | the next group number (§4.4); under `(?n)` none (§6.2) |
| `(?:X)` | `X` | none |
| `(?FLAGS:X)` | `X` with the options set for its body only | none (§6.2) |

<a id="s5-7-p2"></a>[5.7¶2] A group nests at most 250 deep (`PCREC_MAX_GROUP_DEPTH`); one more is refused ("parentheses are too deeply nested"). `()` is a capturing group that matches the empty string. An option setting `(?i)` inside a group lasts to the end of that group, across later alternatives of the group (§6.2).

<a id="s5-8"></a>
### 5.8 `^` and `$`

| spelling | matches the empty string | quantifiable | module |
|---|---|---|---|
| `^` | at position 0 of the subject only, whatever `startpos` is | no | base |
| `$` | at the end of the subject, or before a `\n` that is the last character of the subject | no | base |
| `^` under `(?m)` | also right after any `\n` that is not the last character of the subject | no | `assertions` (§7.1) |
| `$` under `(?m)` | also right before any `\n` | no | `assertions` (§7.1) |

<a id="s5-8-p1"></a>[5.8¶1] `a$` on `a\n` → `[0, 1)`; on `a\n\n` no match; on `a\r\n` no match: only `\n` is a newline for `^`, `$`, `.`, `\Z` and `\N`. `^a` from `startpos` 1 on `ba` is no match; `\G` (§7.1) is the assertion that anchors at `startpos`.

<a id="s6"></a>
## 6. The default modules

<a id="s6-p1"></a>[6¶1] `classes` and `modifiers` are the set `std1`, enabled by every compile that does not name its own `--features` (§2.3).

<a id="s6-1"></a>
### 6.1 Module `classes`

| spelling | matches one character in | engines | quantifiable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `\d` | `[0-9]` | any | yes |
| `\D` | not `\d` | any | yes |
| `\s` | `[\t\n\x0b\f\r ]` | any | yes |
| `\S` | not `\s` | any | yes |
| `\w` | `[A-Za-z0-9_]` | any | yes |
| `\W` | not `\w` | any | yes |
| `\h` | under `byte` `[\t \xa0]`; under `utf8` U+0009, U+0020, U+00A0, U+1680, U+180E, U+2000-U+200A, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 | any | yes |
| `\H` | not `\h` | any | yes |
| `\v` | under `byte` `[\n\x0b\f\r\x85]`; under `utf8` U+000A-U+000D, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029 | any | yes |
| `\V` | not `\v` | any | yes |
| `\N` | not `\n`, whatever `(?s)` says; refused inside a class | any | yes |
| `[[:name:]]` | the POSIX set `name` (below); only inside a class | any | yes |
| `[[:^name:]]` | the complement of the POSIX set `name` | any | yes |

<a id="s6-1-p1"></a>[6.1¶1] The POSIX names and their sets, without UCP: `alnum` `[0-9A-Za-z]`, `alpha` `[A-Za-z]`, `ascii` `[\x00-\x7f]`, `blank` `[\t ]`, `cntrl` `[\x00-\x1f\x7f]`, `digit` `[0-9]`, `graph` `[\x21-\x7e]`, `lower` `[a-z]`, `print` `[\x20-\x7e]`, `punct` the 32 characters of `graph` that are not `alnum`, `space` `[\t\n\x0b\f\r ]`, `upper` `[A-Z]`, `word` `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, `xdigit` `[0-9A-Fa-f]`. Any other name is refused ("unknown POSIX class name").

1. <a id="s6-1-p2"></a>[6.1¶2] The sets above are the same under `byte` and `utf8`: `\w` does not match `é` under `-e utf8` unless UCP is on. Under UCP (§7.8) `\d \s \w` and the POSIX sets are Unicode property sets (`cli.md` §1.9). `\h \H \v \V` do not depend on UCP.
2. <a id="s6-1-p3"></a>[6.1¶3] A negated escape (`\D`, `\S`, `\W`, `\H`, `\V`) and `\N` match only well-formed characters under `utf8`.
3. <a id="s6-1-p4"></a>[6.1¶4] Under `-i` a POSIX `lower` or `upper` set matches both cases (`(?i)[[:upper:]]` matches `a`), except under UCP (`cli.md` §1.9¶5); `\d \s \w` have no case.
4. <a id="s6-1-p5"></a>[6.1¶5] Every set above, on every byte `0x00`-`0xFF` under `-e byte`, is libpcre2's set at options `0`.

<a id="s6-2"></a>
### 6.2 Module `modifiers`

<a id="s6-2-p1"></a>[6.2¶1] An option setting changes how the rest of the pattern is read. `(?LETTERS)` sets options from that point to the end of the enclosing group (or of the pattern), including the group's later alternatives: `a(?i)b|c` matches `aB` and `C` and not `AB`. `(?LETTERS:X)` sets them for `X` only. `(?LETTERS-LETTERS)` sets the letters before `-` and unsets those after; `(?^LETTERS)` first resets `i m n r s x xx U` to off, then sets `LETTERS`; `-` may not follow `^`. `(?)` and `(?-)` change nothing.

| letter | meaning | module |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | caseless: a literal, a class or a backreference matches every case partner under the encoding's fold (`cli.md` §1.8) | `modifiers` |
| `m` | multiline `^` and `$` (§5.8) | `assertions` (§7.1) |
| `s` | `.` matches `\n` (§5.4) | `modifiers` |
| `x` | extended: whitespace and `#` comments ignored (§3.2) | `modifiers` |
| `xx` | `x`, and space and tab ignored inside a class (§3.2); `-x` unsets both | `modifiers` |
| `n` | no auto-capture: `(X)` is `(?:X)`; named groups (§7.5) still capture | `modifiers` |
| `U` | ungreedy: a quantifier without `?` is lazy and one with `?` is greedy; a possessive quantifier (`+` suffix) stays greedy (`(?U)a*+` on `aaa` → `[0, 3)`) | `modifiers` |
| `J` | duplicate group names allowed (§7.5); survives `(?^)` | `backrefs` (§7.3) |
| `a` | `(?aD)`, `(?aS)`, `(?aW)`, `(?aP)`, `(?aT)`, or `(?a)` for all five: restrict a family of sets to ASCII under UCP (`cli.md` §1.9¶4); no effect without UCP; survives `(?^)` | `modifiers` |
| `r` | caseless matching restricted to ASCII-with-ASCII and non-ASCII-with-non-ASCII; under `byte` it changes nothing; under `utf8` it is refused ("not implemented under encoding 'utf8'") | `modifiers` |

1. <a id="s6-2-p2"></a>[6.2¶2] Any other letter is refused ("unrecognized character after (? or (?-"), and an unclosed setting is refused.
2. <a id="s6-2-p3"></a>[6.2¶3] A letter whose module is not enabled is refused naming that module: `(?m)a` under `std1` is refused with `inline option 'm' (multiline) requires module 'assertions'`, even with no `^` or `$` in the pattern. Only SETTING a letter is gated: unsetting one (`(?-m)a` under `std1`, `(?-J)a`, `(?-r)a` under `utf8`) compiles, since it turns on nothing the module owns. So `(?m)` needs `assertions` and `(?J)` needs `backrefs` besides `modifiers`, while `--list-syntax` names only `modifiers` on their rows (the row dispatches the option run; the letter names its own module).
3. <a id="s6-2-p4"></a>[6.2¶4] `-i` on the command line sets the same matching mode as `(?i)` at the start of the pattern, as a compile option rather than a construct: it is not gated, and works with `modifiers` disabled (§2.3¶5a). There is no command-line spelling of the other letters (§2.5).
4. <a id="s6-2-p5"></a>[6.2¶5] `(?n)` applies from where it is written to the end of its scope; a group opened before it, or after its scope closes, still captures: `(a(?n)(b))(c)` on `abc` → group 1 `[0, 2)` (the outer group), group 2 `[2, 3)` (the `(c)`).

<a id="s7"></a>
## 7. Opt-in modules

<a id="s7-p1"></a>[7¶1] Each module in this section has producers and is enabled by naming it in `--features` (or by `all`); `ucp` and `unicode-props` are also enabled by `-e utf8` (§2.3).

<a id="s7-1"></a>
### 7.1 Module `assertions`

<a id="s7-1-p1"></a>[7.1¶1] Each construct matches the empty string at a position that satisfies its condition.

| spelling | condition at position `p` | engines | quantifiable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `\b` | exactly one of the characters before `p` and at `p` is a word character, the subject's ends counting as non-word | any | no |
| `\B` | not `\b` | any | no |
| `\A` | `p` is 0, whatever `startpos` is | any | no |
| `\Z` | `p` is the end of the subject, or `p` is before a `\n` that is the subject's last character | any | no |
| `\z` | `p` is the end of the subject | any | no |
| `\G` | `p` is `startpos` | any | no |
| `\K` | always true; sets the start of the reported match to `p` | vm | no |
| `(?m)` | the option letter that changes `^` and `$` (§5.8) | any | — |

1. <a id="s7-1-p2"></a>[7.1¶2] The word characters for `\b` and `\B` are `\w`'s set (§6.1): ASCII without UCP, so under `byte` `\b\xe9` on `a\xe9` → `[1, 2)`. Under UCP they are Unicode's word set under `byte` (Latin-1) and refused under `utf8` (`cli.md` §1.9¶7).
2. <a id="s7-1-p3"></a>[7.1¶3] `\K` changes only the reported start: `a\Kb` on `ab` → `[1, 2)`; `(a\Kb)` on `ab` → `[1, 2)`, group 1 `[0, 2)`. `\K` inside any lookaround is refused ("not allowed inside a lookaround").
3. <a id="s7-1-p4"></a>[7.1¶4] Inside a class, `\b` is U+0008 (§5.5) and the others are refused.

<a id="s7-2"></a>
### 7.2 Module `atomic-groups`

| spelling | matches | engines | quantifiable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(?>X)` | the first way `X` matches at this position (§4.2); if what follows fails, no other way of `X` is tried | vm | yes |
| `X*+`, `X++`, `X?+`, `X{n,m}+`, `X{n,}+`, `X{,m}+`, `X{n}+` | `(?>X*)`, `(?>X+)` and so on | vm | no |

<a id="s7-2-p1"></a>[7.2¶1] `(?>a|ab)c` on `abc` is no match; `a++a` on `aaa` is no match; `a{1,2}+a` on `aaa` → `[0, 3)`. A possessive quantifier is a quantifier, so a further quantifier after it is refused (`a*+?`). `(*atomic:X)` is the same construct in PCRE2 and is refused as part of module `verbs` (§8.1).

<a id="s7-3"></a>
### 7.3 Module `backrefs`

<a id="s7-3-p1"></a>[7.3¶1] A backreference matches exactly the text the referenced group holds at that point on the current path (§4.4). If the group is unset, the backreference fails. Under `-i` the comparison folds by the encoding's fold (`cli.md` §1.8¶6): `(a)\1` under `-i` on `aA` → `[0, 2)`.

| spelling | refers to | engines |
|---|---|---|
| `\N`, `\NN...` | group N, by the digit rule below | vm |
| `\gN`, `\g{N}` | group N | vm |
| `\g{-N}`, `\g-N` | the Nth group counting back from this point: `(a)\g{-1}` is group 1 | vm |
| `\g{+N}` | the Nth group counting forward from this point | vm |
| `\k<name>`, `\k'name'`, `\k{name}`, `\g{name}`, `(?P=name)` | the group named `name` (§7.5) | vm |
| `\0`, `\0o`, `\0oo` | not a backreference: an octal character (§5.2) | any |
| `(?J)` | the option allowing duplicate names (§7.5) | any |

1. <a id="s7-3-p2"></a>[7.3¶2] The digit rule. After `\`, take the whole run of decimal digits as N. If the run starts with `0` it is octal (§5.2). Otherwise, if N < 10, or the pattern has at least N capturing groups in total, it is a backreference to group N; otherwise the leading octal digits (at most three) are an octal character and the rest of the run is literal digits. So `(a)\10` is `(a)` then U+0008; `(a)\11` on `a\t` → `[0, 2)`; `\18` is U+0001 then `8`; ten groups then `\10` is a backreference to group 10.
2. <a id="s7-3-p3"></a>[7.3¶3] A backreference to a group the pattern does not have is refused, by number (`(a)\2`, "refers to capture group 2, but this pattern has 1"), by relative position (`\g{0}`, `(a)\g{-2}`) or by name (`\k<m>` with no group `m`). `\8` and `\9` in a pattern with fewer groups are refused the same way.
3. <a id="s7-3-p4"></a>[7.3¶4] A reference to a group that has not run yet on the path fails rather than matching empty: `\1(a)` on `aa` is no match; `(a\1)` on `aa` is no match. A group may be referenced before it is written, and the reference sees its value from an earlier iteration: `(a\2|b)(c)` on `bcac` → `[0, 2)`.
4. <a id="s7-3-p5"></a>[7.3¶5] With duplicate names (`(?J)`), a by-name reference refers to the lowest-numbered group of that name that is set: `(?J)(?<n>a)(?<n>b)\k<n>` on `aba` → `[0, 3)`.
5. <a id="s7-3-p6"></a>[7.3¶6] A backreference inside a lookbehind is refused (§7.4).
6. <a id="s7-3-p7"></a>[7.3¶7] Inside a class, `\1`-`\7`, `\8`, `\9`, `\g` and `\k` are base-tier characters (§5.5).

<a id="s7-4"></a>
### 7.4 Module `lookaround`

<a id="s7-4-p1"></a>[7.4¶1] A lookaround matches the empty string at `p` when its condition holds; it consumes nothing.

| spelling | condition | engines | quantifiable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(?=X)`, `(*pla:X)`, `(*positive_lookahead:X)` | `X` matches starting at `p` | vm | yes |
| `(?!X)`, `(*nla:X)`, `(*negative_lookahead:X)` | `X` does not match starting at `p` | vm | yes |
| `(?<=X)`, `(*plb:X)`, `(*positive_lookbehind:X)` | `X` matches ending at `p` | vm | yes |
| `(?<!X)`, `(*nlb:X)`, `(*negative_lookbehind:X)` | `X` does not match ending at `p` | vm | yes |
| `(?*X)`, `(*napla:X)`, `(*non_atomic_positive_lookahead:X)` | as `(?=X)`, non-atomic | vm | yes |
| `(?<*X)`, `(*naplb:X)`, `(*non_atomic_positive_lookbehind:X)` | as `(?<=X)`, non-atomic | vm | yes |

1. <a id="s7-4-p2"></a>[7.4¶2] A positive lookaround is atomic: the first way its body matches is kept, and a later failure does not retry the body. `(?=(a|ab))\1c` on `abc` is no match, while the non-atomic `(?*(a|ab))\1c` on `abc` → `[0, 3)`, group 1 `[0, 2)`.
2. <a id="s7-4-p3"></a>[7.4¶3] Groups inside a positive lookaround keep the values of the way that succeeded (`(?=(a))a` on `a` → group 1 `[0, 1)`); groups inside a negative lookaround are unset after it (`(?!(a))b` on `b` → group 1 unset).
3. <a id="s7-4-p4"></a>[7.4¶4] A lookbehind reads characters before `p` even when they are before `startpos` (`(?<=b)a` from `startpos` 1 on `ba` → `[1, 2)`).
4. <a id="s7-4-p5"></a>[7.4¶5] Every top-level alternative of a lookbehind's body must match a fixed number of characters; different alternatives may differ (`(?<=a|bc)x` compiles). A body that can match a varying number of characters within one alternative is refused with a capability diagnostic (shape 5): `(?<=(a|bc))x`, `(?<=a+)x`, and any lookbehind containing a backreference (`(a)(?<=\1)`). Fixed counts are characters, so `(?<=é)a` under `utf8` on `éa` → `[2, 3)`. An alternative may itself be a group of alternatives when they share one length: `(?<=(?:ab|cd)|e)x` and `(?<=(?i:ab|cd))x` compile, while `(?<=(?:a|bc))x` is variable and refused like `(?<=(a|bc))x`.
5. <a id="s7-4-p5a"></a>[7.4¶5a] A subroutine call inside a lookbehind (§7.7) is measured through the called group. A lookbehind whose call re-enters a group containing that lookbehind, directly or through the called groups' own calls, has no length and is refused, as libpcre2 refuses it: `(?<=(?R))x`, `((?<=(?1))a)`, `((?<=(?2))a)(b|(?1))`. A call inside a nested lookahead is not followed (`(?<=a(?=(?R)))x` and `((?<=(?2)))(a(?=(?1)))` compile); a call inside a nested lookbehind is (`((?<=(?2)))(a(?<=(?1)))` is refused). `(a)(?<=(?1))` compiles.
6. <a id="s7-4-p6"></a>[7.4¶6] A quantifier on a lookaround means the assertion is optional when its minimum is 0 and required once otherwise: `(?=a)*b` on `b` → `[0, 1)`, `(?=a){2}a` on `a` → `[0, 1)`.
6. <a id="s7-4-p7"></a>[7.4¶7] There is no non-atomic negative lookaround: `(*nanla:...)` and `(*nanlb:...)` are refused ("(*alpha_assertion) not recognized"), as PCRE2 refuses them. `\K` inside any lookaround is refused (§7.1).

<a id="s7-5"></a>
### 7.5 Module `named-groups`

| spelling | matches | captures |
|---|---|---|
| `(?<name>X)`, `(?'name'X)`, `(?P<name>X)` | `X` | the next group number, and the name `name` |

1. <a id="s7-5-p1"></a>[7.5¶1] A name is an ASCII letter or `_` followed by ASCII letters, digits and `_`, at most 128 bytes (`PCREC_MAX_GROUP_NAME`). A name starting with a digit is refused; a longer name is refused. Under `-e utf8` a name character may also be any letter (`\p{L}`), and after the first any decimal digit (`\p{Nd}`): `(?<é>a)\k<é>` compiles; the limit stays 128 bytes. Under `-e byte` a byte above `\x7f` is never a name character. `rx_info.groups` carries the name's bytes as written.
2. <a id="s7-5-p2"></a>[7.5¶2] A named group is numbered with the unnamed ones, by position (§4.4): `(?<n>a)(?<n2>b)(c)` on `abc` → groups 1, 2, 3.
3. <a id="s7-5-p3"></a>[7.5¶3] Two groups with one name are refused ("two named subpatterns have the same name") unless `(?J)` is in effect at the second declaration (§6.2); `(?<n>a)|(?J)(?<n>b)` compiles.
4. <a id="s7-5-p4"></a>[7.5¶4] How a caller finds a group by name is `match_api.md` §5.4; how a library definition's names reach a caller is `match_api.md` §5.5.
5. <a id="s7-5-p5"></a>[7.5¶5] `(?<` followed by `=`, `!` or `*` is a lookbehind (§7.4), not a name.

<a id="s7-6"></a>
### 7.6 Module `quoting`

<a id="s7-6-p1"></a>[7.6¶1] `\Q` begins quoting and `\E` ends it. Every character between them is a literal, `\` included: `\Qa.b\E.` matches `a.b` followed by any character, and `\Q\\E` matches one `\`.

1. <a id="s7-6-p2"></a>[7.6¶2] A `\Q` with no `\E` quotes to the end of the pattern. A `\E` with no `\Q` is ignored (`a\E` matches `a`).
2. <a id="s7-6-p3"></a>[7.6¶3] Quoting is transparent to the item structure: a quantifier after `\E` applies to the last quoted character (`\Qab\E+` matches `abb`), and an empty `\Q\E` is nothing (`a\Q\E*` is `a*`).
3. <a id="s7-6-p4"></a>[7.6¶4] Inside quotes, `(?x)` whitespace and `#` are literals (`(?x)\Qa b\E` matches `a b`).
4. <a id="s7-6-p5"></a>[7.6¶5] Inside a class, `\Q...\E` quotes members: `[\Qa-c\E]` matches `a`, `-` and `c` and not `b`; `[\Q]\E]` matches `]`.
5. <a id="s7-6-p6"></a>[7.6¶6] Quoting is lexical: it never makes a group, so `(a\Qb)c\E)` quotes `b)c` and the final `)` closes the group.

<a id="s7-7"></a>
### 7.7 Module `recursion`

<a id="s7-7-p1"></a>[7.7¶1] A subroutine call matches the called group's pattern at the current position, as if its text were written there, with the options in effect where the group is written.

| spelling | calls | engines |
|---|---|---|
| `(?R)`, `(?0)`, `\g<0>`, `\g'0'` | the whole pattern | vm |
| `(?N)`, `\g<N>`, `\g'N'` | group N | vm |
| `(?+N)`, `(?-N)`, `\g<+N>`, `\g<-N>`, `\g'+N'`, `\g'-N'` | the Nth group counting forward or back from the call | vm |
| `(?&name)`, `(?P>name)`, `\g<name>`, `\g'name'` | the group named `name` | vm |
| `(?(DEFINE)X)` | nothing: `X` never runs where it is written and exists to be called | any |

1. <a id="s7-7-p2"></a>[7.7¶2] Digits are read as one decimal number, so a leading zero does not change it: `(?01)` and `\g<01>` call group 1, while `(?00)` and `\g<00>` call the whole pattern. `(?10)` and `(?-10)` are multi-digit calls.
2. <a id="s7-7-p3"></a>[7.7¶3] A call to a group the pattern does not have is refused (`(a)(?2)`; `(?-1)(a)` counts back past the first group).
3. <a id="s7-7-p4"></a>[7.7¶4] A call is not atomic: a later failure backtracks into it. `^(a|ab)(?1)c$` on `aabc` → `[0, 4)`.
4. <a id="s7-7-p5"></a>[7.7¶5] Groups set inside a call are restored when the call returns; the call leaves the caller's groups as they were before it. `(a|b)(?1)` on `ab` → group 1 `[0, 1)`.
5. <a id="s7-7-p6"></a>[7.7¶6] `(?(DEFINE)X)` must have one alternative; `(?(DEFINE)a|c)` is refused. Groups inside `X` are numbered in place; a call into them restores them on return (item 4), so they are never set on the reported path: `(?(DEFINE)(?<d>\d+))(?&d)-(?&d)` on `12-34` → `[0, 5)`, group 1 unset.
6. <a id="s7-7-p7"></a>[7.7¶7] Each call that the artifact keeps as a call (rather than writing the group's text in place, `tuning.md` §2.9) uses a resume frame, so call depth is bounded by the artifact's frame and trail capacities and an exhausted capacity is the give-up `PCREC_ERR_FRAMES` (`limits.md` §3.2, §4). Left recursion is `limits.md` §6. A call whose group can never complete (`(?R)` alone) answers no match.

<a id="s7-8"></a>
### 7.8 Module `ucp`

| spelling | meaning | engines |
|---|---|---|
| `(*UCP)` at the start of the pattern | UCP semantics, as `--ucp` | any |
| `(*UTF)`, `(*UTF8)` at the start of the pattern | confirm `-e utf8`; refused under `byte` ("requires --encoding=utf8") | any |

1. <a id="s7-8-p1"></a>[7.8¶1] Start-of-pattern options must precede every other item, in any order (`(*UCP)(*UTF)` and `(*UTF)(*UCP)` are both accepted); elsewhere they are refused ("(*VERB) not recognized or malformed").
2. <a id="s7-8-p2"></a>[7.8¶2] What UCP changes — `\d \s \w`, the POSIX classes, `\b \B`, and the caseless fold of the POSIX case sets — and which UCP sets are refused under `utf8`, is `cli.md` §1.9 and `limits.md` §3.8. Under `byte`, UCP sets are their Unicode sets clamped to `0x00`-`0xFF`: `--ucp` `\w` matches `\xe9`, `[[:alpha:]]` matches `\xaa`, `\d` does not match `\xb2`.
3. <a id="s7-8-p3"></a>[7.8¶3] `--ucp` and `(*UCP)` need module `ucp` enabled under `byte`; `-e utf8` enables it.

<a id="s7-9"></a>
### 7.9 Module `unicode-props`

| spelling | matches one character | engines | quantifiable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `\p{X}` | with property `X` | any | yes |
| `\P{X}`, `\p{^X}` | without property `X` (`\P{^X}` is `\p{X}`) | any | yes |

<a id="s7-9-p1"></a>[7.9¶1] The accepted names (general categories, `L&`/`Lc`, `Any`, `Xan Xps Xsp Xuc Xwd`, scripts in three namespaces, the binary properties, `Bidi_Class`, and the Block and Age extensions beyond PCRE2), their case and separator rules, the clamping under `byte` and the refused names are `cli.md` §1.17.1. Under `-i`, `\p{Lu}`, `\p{Ll}` and `\p{Lt}` are `\p{L&}` (`cli.md` §1.8¶5). A property escape is valid inside a class. A malformed escape (`\p` with no name) is refused. The tables are Unicode 16.0.0.

<a id="s7-10"></a>
### 7.10 Module `vars`

<a id="s7-10-p1"></a>[7.10¶1] `${name}` matches, literally, the bytes the caller passes for variable `name` in the call that runs the match; `${name:-word}` and the other bash-shaped forms supply defaults. The spelling, the caller's array, the refusals and the engine are `vars.md` §2-§7. Without the module, `${` is refused (`requires module 'vars'`) anywhere outside a class; PCRE2 reads the same text as `$` followed by literals, which can never match. Inside a class, `$` and `{` are literals (`[${]` matches `{`).

<a id="s7-11"></a>
### 7.11 Module `callouts`

<a id="s7-11-p1"></a>[7.11¶1] `(?C)`, `(?Cn)` (`n` 0-255; `(?C)` is `(?C0)`) and `(?C"name")` call the user's code at that point of the match: a numbered callout calls `rx_callout_<n>`, a named one `rx_callout_<name>`, each bound by the user's C (`match_api.md` §11). Every PCRE2 string delimiter is accepted for the name (`` ` `` `'` `"` `^` `%` `#` `$` and `{...}`). The string is a C identifier with optional attributes after commas: `(?C"name,consume")`, `(?C"name,once")`. A numbered callout's attributes are declared beside the pattern (`cli.md` §1.21, `rxt_format.md` §1.5¶13a). A callout pattern compiles to the VM engine.

<a id="s7-11-p2"></a>[7.11¶2] The callee's return decides the path: `0` continues, `-1` backtracks, a `consume` callee's positive return consumes that many bytes (`match_api.md` §11.4). A callout cannot be quantified (PCRE2's rule too); wrap it in a group.

<a id="s7-11-p3"></a>[7.11¶3] Refused: a malformed `(?C` (a number above 255, a number followed by other text, an unsupported delimiter, an unterminated string), with or without the module; a name containing `__`; a name that is not a C identifier; a name whose binding symbol is a name the artifact's shared ABI block already declares (`(?C"ref")`, whose `rx_callout_ref` is the bindings' own type; `match_api.md` §11.2); an empty or repeated attribute; the attribute `verify` (not implemented yet); `once` on a site that can fire twice in one attempt (`match_api.md` §11.8, with the table of what to change, §11.8¶3); a callout inside a lookbehind (a `consume` site there is refused first, as a lookbehind whose length is not fixed), inside a conditional's condition, or inside a group reached by a subroutine call or recursion.

<a id="s8"></a>
## 8. Recognised constructs without a producer, and excluded ones

<a id="s8-1"></a>
### 8.1 Not built

<a id="s8-1-p1"></a>[8.1¶1] These are real PCRE2 constructs, each owned by the module named; no producer exists in this build. With the module not enabled the refusal is shape 1 (`requires module 'X'`); with it enabled, shape 2 (`module 'X' is enabled but ... is not implemented yet`), except module `verbs`, whose refusal is `(*...) requires module 'verbs'` at every gate state.

| spelling | PCRE2 meaning | module |
|---|---|---|
| `(?\|X\|Y)` | branch reset: alternatives reuse the same group numbers | `branch-reset` |
| `(?#text)` | a comment up to the next `)` | `comments` |
| `(?(N)Y\|N)`, `(?(<name>)…)`, `(?('name')…)`, `(?(R)…)`, `(?(assert)…)` | conditional group | `conditionals` |
| `(?[...])` | extended class with set operations | `extended-classes` |
| `\R` | any newline sequence | `misc` |
| `\X` | an extended grapheme cluster | `misc` |
| `\C` | one code unit | `misc` |
| `\cX` | the control character `X` (uppercased) xor `0x40` | `misc` |
| `\o{ooo}` | the character with that octal code | `misc` |
| `\N{U+h...}` | the code point `h...` | `unicode-props` |
| `(*ACCEPT)`, `(*FAIL)`, `(*F)` | backtracking control | `verbs` |
| `(*CR)`, `(*LF)`, `(*CRLF)`, `(*ANYCRLF)`, `(*ANY)`, `(*NUL)`, `(*BSR_ANYCRLF)`, `(*BSR_UNICODE)`, `(*NOTEMPTY)`, `(*NOTEMPTY_ATSTART)` | start-of-pattern newline and match options | `verbs` |
| `(*atomic:X)`, `(*sr:X)`, `(*script_run:X)`, `(*asr:X)`, `(*atomic_script_run:X)` | atomic group, script runs | `verbs` |

<a id="s8-1-p2"></a>[8.1¶2] `--list-verbs` (`registry.md` §4) is the complete table of `(*NAME)` spellings and which are planned. `(?#...)` is unrelated to `#` comments under `(?x)`, which are base grammar of module `modifiers` (§3.2).

<a id="s8-2"></a>
### 8.2 Excluded

<a id="s8-2-p1"></a>[8.2¶1] These are refused by every build and every gate state. The ones that are real PCRE2 syntax refuse with shape 3; the ones PCRE2 also refuses refuse with a grammar diagnostic (shape 7).

| spelling | refusal |
|---|---|
| `(*COMMIT)`, `(*PRUNE)`, `(*SKIP)`, `(*THEN)`, each also with `:NAME`; `(*MARK:NAME)`, `(*:NAME)` | shape 3 |
| `(*NO_AUTO_POSSESS)`, `(*NO_DOTSTAR_ANCHOR)`, `(*NO_JIT)`, `(*NO_START_OPT)`, `(*CASELESS_RESTRICT)`, `(*TURKISH_CASING)` | shape 3 |
| `(*LIMIT_MATCH=d)`, `(*LIMIT_DEPTH=d)`, `(*LIMIT_HEAP=d)`, `(*LIMIT_RECURSION=d)` | shape 3; the match budgets are compile options (`limits.md` §3.1) |
| `(*scs:...)`, `(*scan_substring:...)` | shape 3 |
| `(*NAME)` with a name in neither verb table | shape 7, "(*VERB) not recognized or malformed" |
| `(*nanla:...)`, `(*nanlb:...)`, any other unknown lowercase name | shape 7, "(*alpha_assertion) not recognized" |
| `\N{name}`, `\F`, `\L`, `\l`, `\U`, `\u` | shape 7 |
| `[[.x.]]`, `[[=x=]]` | shape 7 (§5.5) |
| `(?P` followed by anything but `<`, `=` or `>` | shape 7 |
| `(?` followed by a character that begins no construct (`(?q)`) | shape 7 |

<a id="s9"></a>
## 9. Where pcrec's answer differs from libpcre2's

<a id="s9-p1"></a>[9¶1] The compliance page (`docs/pcre2_compliance.md`) is the construct-by-construct delta; this section lists every difference this document states, at the option mapping of §1.2.

1. <a id="s9-p2"></a>[9¶2] Refusals of accepted syntax. Every construct of §8.1, every construct whose module a compile does not enable, and these capability and grammar refusals: a lookbehind alternative of varying length, or containing a backreference (§7.4), including a group of alternatives of different lengths (`(?<=(?:a|bc))x`), which libpcre2 accepts as a variable-length lookbehind; `(?r)` under `utf8` (§6.2); the wide UCP sets and UCP `\b \B` under `utf8` (§7.8); `${` outside a class without module `vars` (§7.10); a pattern over a compile budget (§2.4 shape 6).
2. <a id="s9-p3"></a>[9¶3] Give-ups. A VM artifact may answer `PCREC_ERR_STEPS`, `PCREC_ERR_FRAMES` or `PCREC_ERR_WORK` where libpcre2 answers (§4.6), including the left recursions where libpcre2 concludes no match (`limits.md` §6).
3. <a id="s9-p4"></a>[9¶4] A recursion with no way to complete. `(?R)` alone, on any subject, is no match under pcrec; libpcre2 returns its recursion-loop error.
   - <a id="s9-p4a"></a>[9¶4a] More generally, where libpcre2's recursion-loop check fires (`PCRE2_ERROR_RECURSELOOP`) because a call can re-enter its own group without consuming, pcrec's matcher runs the search instead and answers a match, no match or a give-up (§4.6): `(?:a|(?R))+` on `a` → `[0, 1)`, on `aa` → `[0, 2)`, on `b` `PCREC_ERR_FRAMES`; `((?1)?a)` on `a` → `[0, 1)`.
4. <a id="s9-p5"></a>[9¶5] A start position beyond the subject. `startpos > n` returns no match; libpcre2 returns an offset error (`match_api.md` §9.2¶4).
   - <a id="s9-p5a"></a>[9¶5a] A start position inside a character under `utf8` (`.` on `éa` from `startpos` 1) returns `PCREC_ERR_STARTPOS`; libpcre2 with `PCRE2_MATCH_INVALID_UTF` searches on from the next character (`[2, 3)`) (`match_api.md` §9.2).
5. <a id="s9-p6"></a>[9¶6] Module `vars`. With the module enabled, `${name}` and its forms are pcrec syntax with no PCRE2 meaning (§7.10).
6. <a id="s9-p7"></a>[9¶7] — retired (moved to §6.2¶3).
7. <a id="s9-p8"></a>[9¶8] — retired (the difference is gone; §3.2¶2).
8. <a id="s9-p9"></a>[9¶9] Module `callouts`. pcrec's answer for a callout pattern is the backtracking-order answer; libpcre2's moves with its optimizations, so the two agree where libpcre2's answer does not depend on them (`match_api.md` §11.6). A `consume` callout and the binding by symbol have no PCRE2 form.
